title: Summit Provider Network x Redwood — Private/VPC technical deep dive
topics: Private deployment modes (VPC vs on-prem) and shared responsibility
VPC networking: PrivateLink/peering, egress allowlists, DNS/TLS
Audit logging and SIEM export (Splunk) + retention
KMS/HSM integration points and encryption boundaries
Performance sizing: concurrency, throughput, TTFT, batching/caching
PHI constraints and data handling assumptions
summary: Summit Provider Network platform/security team walked through their target PHI workloads (clinical note summarization + search/QA) and asked detailed questions about Redwood Private in a customer VPC: connectivity options (PrivateLink vs peering), outbound-only operation, DNS/TLS requirements, logging/audit export into Splunk, and key management (customer-managed KMS; HSM as an option depending on environment). Redwood outlined the Private architecture boundaries (control plane vs data plane), what logs are available today and typical retention/export patterns, and how performance is sized (tokens/sec targets, concurrency, context length distribution, TTFT). Agreed to share a reference architecture diagram, a short network prerequisites checklist, and a sizing worksheet; Summit to provide representative request traces (prompt length, max tokens, concurrency) and security questionnaire sections focused on logging/retention.
next_steps: Redwood (Simran) to send Summit a Private/VPC reference architecture diagram + network prerequisites checklist (PrivateLink/peering options, DNS/TLS, egress allowlists).
Summit (Elena/Maya) to send Redwood sample workload metrics: expected QPS/concurrency, prompt/context length distribution, max output tokens, and latency SLOs.
Redwood (Colin) to draft an initial sizing recommendation (GPU count/profile + batching/caching assumptions) for a 2–3 week evaluation.
Redwood (Marcus) to confirm current audit log fields + supported export formats and share Splunk-forwarding pattern (docs + example).
Hannah to coordinate a follow-up 30-min security Q&A with Tom + GRC/legal stakeholders once NDA is confirmed.
transcript:
Meeting: Summit Provider Network x Redwood — Private/VPC technical deep dive
Recorded: 2026-01-28 3:00 PM ET
Duration: 56 min

Attendees
- Hannah Schmitt (Redwood, AE)
- Colin O'Donnell (Redwood, Solutions Engineering)
- Simran Kaur (Redwood, Reference Architect)
- Marcus Lin (Redwood, Security Engineering)
- Maya Patel (Summit, Director Platform Eng)
- Tom Becker (Summit, Security Architect)
- Elena Ruiz (Summit, Data Eng Lead)
- Dr. Priya Nair (Summit, Clinical Informatics)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Discussed Redwood Private deployment in Summit-managed VPC, network connectivity, and data plane boundaries.
- Reviewed audit logging, retention, and SIEM (Splunk) integration expectations.
- Covered sizing and performance assumptions (context length, concurrency, TTFT vs total latency).

Action items (auto-generated)
- Simran to send VPC reference architecture + checklist.
- Elena to share sample payload characteristics and volume estimates.
- Marcus to follow up on audit log export details.


Transcript

[00:00] Hannah Schmitt: Cool. Alright, we’re at the top of the hour. Thanks everyone for making time. This is the technical deep dive on Private deployment in your VPC. I’m Hannah, I work with Colin and Simran and Marcus here.

[00:12] Maya Patel: Yep, thanks Hannah.

[00:14] Colin O'Donnell: Hey everyone.

[00:15] Simran Kaur: Hi.

[00:17] Marcus Lin: Hello.

[00:18] Tom Becker: Hey.

[00:19] Elena Ruiz: Hi.

[00:20] Dr. Priya Nair: Hello.

[00:23] Hannah Schmitt: Goal today is less “pitch” and more, like, answer the architecture questions you sent over: VPC networking assumptions, logging into Splunk, key management, and performance sizing. If we don’t get through everything we’ll capture it.

[00:38] Maya Patel: Perfect. Maybe I’ll start with the current situation so you can anchor. We have two main use cases. One is clinical summarization for providers, think discharge notes, visit notes. The other is semantic search / question answering over a knowledge base that includes some PHI.

[00:56] Dr. Priya Nair: And just to be clear, a lot of these prompts include identifiable info, so we’re assuming this is a HIPAA context.

[01:03] Hannah Schmitt: Yeah, makes sense.

[01:05] Tom Becker: And from security side, we can’t use a public SaaS endpoint for that. We’ve done Azure OpenAI for non-PHI, but for PHI we need it in our network boundary. So that’s why we’re here.

[01:19] Colin O'Donnell: Totally. The short version: Redwood has Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. For your case, Private is the one where the inference data plane runs inside your VPC or on-prem, and you control the network boundary. There’s still a control plane component for updates/telemetry depending on mode, but we can do it outbound-only.

[01:38] Maya Patel: When you say outbound-only, like no inbound from Redwood into our VPC?

[01:42] Simran Kaur: Correct in the common pattern. We deploy components in your VPC—usually Kubernetes-based. The cluster initiates outbound connections to pull artifacts and optionally to reach the control plane for licensing/health, depending on the configuration. Inbound access is your choice, typically through an internal load balancer.

[01:59] Tom Becker: Okay. We have a hard requirement: no inbound from vendor networks, and no public IPs.

[02:05] Simran Kaur: That’s aligned with how most regulated customers do it.

[02:09] Elena Ruiz: Can we talk connectivity options? We have multiple VPCs, we do shared services VPC plus app VPCs. We use VPC peering and sometimes PrivateLink.

[02:20] Simran Kaur: Yep. Common options:
1) Private internal endpoint in the same VPC as your app.
2) If cross-VPC, either VPC peering or Transit Gateway routing.
3) PrivateLink-style pattern if you want a service endpoint exposed to other VPCs without full routing. Implementation depends on cloud.

[02:42] Maya Patel: We’re on AWS primarily. We can do TGW. PrivateLink is preferred for some consumers.

[02:47] Colin O'Donnell: We can work with TGW and also do NLB + PrivateLink for the inference endpoint if you want that pattern. We’d need to confirm the exact topology.

[02:58] Tom Becker: DNS/TLS—how does that work? We require internal DNS names, and certificates managed through ACM Private CA.

[03:07] Simran Kaur: Typically you front the inference service with an internal ALB/NLB. TLS termination can happen there using ACM, yes. We can also do mTLS if your internal standard requires it.

[03:20] Marcus Lin: From a security posture perspective, we’re happy when TLS is terminated within your boundary, and you can enforce cipher suites, cert rotation, etc. If you want the pods to do TLS end-to-end, we can support that too, but it’s usually more ops.

[03:35] Elena Ruiz: Do your SDKs require anything special with DNS? Like, do we need your domain?

[03:39] Colin O'Donnell: No. For Private, you’re essentially pointing your clients at an endpoint you control—like https://llm-internal.summit.local or whatever—and our API surface stays consistent. The hostname is yours.

[03:52] Maya Patel: Okay. Next: egress. We’re strict there too. Can you run fully air-gapped?

[03:58] Simran Kaur: Fully air-gapped is possible in the on-prem package, but it’s a heavier lift and we’d want to scope it. In VPC, we typically require egress to a small set of endpoints for artifact pulls and optionally for license checks. We can provide the allowlist. Some customers mirror artifacts into their own registry/S3 to reduce external egress.

[04:20] Tom Becker: So there is some “phone home” in the default mode.

[04:23] Marcus Lin: I’ll be precise: there are configurations where telemetry is disabled or minimized. For regulated, we often do outbound-only health and update checks. The data plane logs and prompts do not get sent out. But yes, there is a control plane connection unless you choose the offline mode.

[04:39] Tom Becker: Okay, we’ll want the “minimal” option, and we need it documented.

[04:45] Hannah Schmitt: We can share a network prereqs doc and get on a security review call for the exact language.

[04:51] Dr. Priya Nair: For PHI: Are prompts stored anywhere by Redwood?

[04:56] Colin O'Donnell: In Private mode, the requests are handled in your environment. There’s no Redwood-hosted logging of prompts by default. Within your environment, you can configure what you log. If you enable request/response logging, that’s your choice and storage.

[05:12] Marcus Lin: And we can talk about audit logs separately—those are about admin actions, config changes, access, not the full prompt payload.

[05:20] Maya Patel: Good segue. Audit logs and SIEM. We push everything to Splunk. What logs do you have and how do we export?

[05:27] Marcus Lin: There are a few layers:
- Infrastructure logs: Kubernetes/audit, node logs—owned by you.
- Redwood service logs: API gateway logs, control plane events, auth events.
- Audit events: changes in config, model deployments, API key creation, role changes.

[05:45] Tom Becker: We need user attribution for admin actions and API usage. We also need retention controls.

[05:51] Marcus Lin: For admin actions: if you integrate SSO/SAML, we can tie actions to identities and emit audit events. For API usage: we can emit per-request metadata like timestamp, route/model, token counts, latency buckets. We generally avoid logging raw payloads unless you turn it on.

[06:13] Elena Ruiz: Is it JSON logs? Syslog?

[06:16] Marcus Lin: In Private we typically produce structured JSON logs to stdout, and you collect via Fluent Bit / OpenTelemetry collector to Splunk HEC or whatever your pipeline is. We’ve seen Splunk Connect for Kubernetes used a lot.

[06:31] Maya Patel: That’s fine. We already run Fluent Bit.

[06:34] Tom Becker: Are audit logs separate from standard logs? Like, can we ensure they’re immutable?

[06:40] Marcus Lin: We emit them as a stream. Immutability is usually achieved in your storage layer—Splunk retention + WORM storage, or S3 Object Lock, depending on your policy.

[06:52] Tom Becker: Okay. Also: we have a requirement for 1 year retention for audit, 30–90 days for operational logs.

[06:59] Marcus Lin: That’s typically doable. We’ll confirm which fields are present today. I don’t want to overpromise on every field without checking the current build.

[07:08] Colin O'Donnell: We can send an example event schema—redacted.

[07:12] Maya Patel: Great.

[07:13] Elena Ruiz: Another question: RBAC. We have different teams, platform vs app teams. Some can deploy models, others can only call APIs.

[07:22] Colin O'Donnell: Redwood has RBAC at the console/control plane level. In Private, we can define roles like Admin, Operator, Viewer, and you can scope access by project/environment. For API callers, you can use service tokens scoped to specific models/routes.

[07:41] Tom Becker: SSO: SAML with Okta.

[07:43] Marcus Lin: Okta SAML is supported. We can do SCIM provisioning depending on your setup—again, I’ll confirm what’s GA in Private.

[07:52] Hannah Schmitt: We’ll keep the claims safe. We can align on what’s currently generally available versus beta.

[08:00] Maya Patel: Okay. Now key management. We have to use customer-managed keys. KMS in AWS, and for some workloads, HSM-backed keys.

[08:10] Simran Kaur: In the VPC deployment, you can use AWS KMS for encryption at rest for any persistent storage you enable—object storage, volumes, etc. For secrets, you can integrate with Secrets Manager or Vault.

[08:25] Tom Becker: Where does encryption at rest apply? Do you store anything at rest besides container images?

[08:31] Simran Kaur: The inference runtime primarily uses ephemeral memory. At rest you might have: model weights cached on local NVMe/EBS depending on performance, any prompt cache if you enable it, logs, and metrics.

[08:46] Colin O'Donnell: There’s also the KV cache in GPU memory, but that’s not “at rest,” that’s ephemeral. Sometimes transcription writes “KV cash” so, same thing.

[08:55] Elena Ruiz: (laughs) KV cash.

[08:57] Tom Becker: If model weights are stored on disk, do they need to be encrypted?

[09:03] Simran Kaur: Typically yes, we’d recommend encryption on volumes. That’s straightforward with EBS encryption under KMS.

[09:11] Tom Becker: HSM: can we integrate with CloudHSM?

[09:15] Marcus Lin: For most patterns, KMS is the integration point and CloudHSM underpins KMS if you configure it. If you specifically require direct HSM calls from the application, that’s a different integration and we’d need to scope.

[09:29] Tom Becker: Okay, so “HSM-backed KMS” is fine.

[09:32] Marcus Lin: Yes, that’s usually the phrasing.

[09:35] Maya Patel: Now performance. We need to figure out what size of cluster / GPUs. We’re struggling because token stuff is… it’s not like normal microservices.

[09:45] Colin O'Donnell: Totally. Let’s break it down:
- Which model(s)
- Context lengths
- Output lengths
- Concurrency / arrival pattern
- Latency SLO: time-to-first-token (TTFT) vs full completion

[10:03] Dr. Priya Nair: Clinicians care about “first token” a lot. If it starts responding quickly, that feels good.

[10:10] Colin O'Donnell: Exactly. TTFT is what we optimize with routing, KV caching, and batching policies.

[10:18] Elena Ruiz: We’re thinking either a 70B class model or a smaller one tuned for clinical summarization. We haven’t decided.

[10:27] Colin O'Donnell: If you’re open to it, we can start with a strong open model and then evaluate. The difference between, say, 8B/13B vs 70B is massive for GPU footprint.

[10:38] Maya Patel: What are typical GPU types?

[10:41] Colin O'Donnell: In AWS, common are A10G, L4 (depending), A100, H100. For 70B, you’re generally in A100/H100 territory depending on quantization.

[10:54] Elena Ruiz: We’ve used vLLM on A10s for a 13B and it was okay-ish.

[10:59] Colin O'Donnell: Yep, that’s consistent.

[11:02] Maya Patel: Workload numbers: For summarization, peak is like 40 concurrent requests, but each request is large—like 4k to 8k tokens of input.

[11:13] Colin O'Donnell: 4k-8k input. Output?

[11:17] Maya Patel: Maybe 500 to 1,000 tokens.

[11:20] Dr. Priya Nair: Sometimes less, but yeah.

[11:23] Colin O'Donnell: And latency target? Full completion, like under 20 seconds? Under 10?

[11:30] Maya Patel: We want TTFT under 1.5 seconds ideally. Full completion under, say, 15 seconds for typical note.

[11:39] Colin O'Donnell: Great. That’s something we can size to.

[11:44] Elena Ruiz: For search/QA, it’s more like 200 QPS but small prompts, like 200-500 tokens input.

[11:52] Colin O'Donnell: Two very different workloads. Often we split routes—one model/cluster for summarization, another for high-QPS QA.

[12:01] Maya Patel: Can it be one cluster with smart routing?

[12:05] Colin O'Donnell: It can, but you may end up with resource contention because long-context summarization can starve the batch scheduler. Redwood runtime supports continuous batching, but mixing extremes sometimes hurts tail latency.

[12:20] Elena Ruiz: Makes sense.

[12:22] Simran Kaur: Architecturally, it can still be one Private deployment with multiple “pools” or node groups: one GPU pool tuned for long-context, one for short.

[12:33] Maya Patel: Okay.

[12:34] Tom Becker: On performance, do you have any hard numbers? tokens per second per GPU?

[12:41] Colin O'Donnell: We do, but it depends heavily on model, quantization, context length, and batch size. Rather than give a misleading number, the best thing is you send us a small sample trace distribution and we’ll return a sizing estimate with assumptions.

[12:57] Tom Becker: Fair.

[13:00] Elena Ruiz: What about caching? You mentioned prefix caching. If we’re summarizing notes, there isn’t a shared prefix.

[13:07] Colin O'Donnell: True. Prefix cache helps most when you have shared system prompts or repeated context. For QA/search, you might have a consistent system prompt and tool schemas. For summarization, caching is less helpful unless you reuse templates.

[13:23] Maya Patel: We do have a standard instruction template, but the note itself changes.

[13:27] Colin O'Donnell: Still helps a bit, but not as dramatic.

[13:31] Dr. Priya Nair: What about safety filters? We have compliance requirements.

[13:35] Hannah Schmitt: We can talk about that separately, but for Private, you can run your own filters either upstream or as part of your orchestration. Redwood focuses on inference runtime + routing/observability.

[13:47] Maya Patel: Observability: do we get token-level metrics?

[13:51] Colin O'Donnell: Yes. We provide per-route and per-model dashboards—latency breakdowns, TTFT, tokens in/out, error rates. In Private, you can emit metrics into your Prometheus/Grafana or integrate with your existing tooling.

[14:05] Elena Ruiz: Can we export traces? We use OpenTelemetry.

[14:09] Colin O'Donnell: We have tracing hooks. We can emit spans around request lifecycle. Some of that is in active development; we can align on what’s available in the Private package you’d deploy.

[14:22] Tom Becker: Okay. Another networking question: do you require inbound access from our engineers to your control plane? Like a web console hosted by you?

[14:32] Simran Kaur: There are deployment modes:
- “Private data plane, hosted control plane”: you access the console over the internet, but no PHI is there.
- “Private control plane”: console and control services are also deployed in your VPC.
For HIPAA/PHI, many customers still use hosted control plane because it contains config and metrics, not payloads. But if your policy says no, we have the private control plane option.

[14:58] Tom Becker: We prefer private control plane to reduce exceptions.

[15:02] Hannah Schmitt: That’s good to know. It may affect timeline and cost, but we can scope.

[15:08] Maya Patel: What’s the operational model? Who patches what?

[15:12] Simran Kaur: Shared responsibility:
- You operate the Kubernetes cluster, networking, and underlying cloud account.
- Redwood provides the application components, upgrades, and support guidance.
We can do managed upgrade windows and provide validated versions.

[15:30] Elena Ruiz: Do you support EKS?

[15:32] Simran Kaur: Yes, EKS is common.

[15:36] Maya Patel: We have strict change management. We need predictable upgrade cadence.

[15:41] Hannah Schmitt: That’s consistent with regulated deployments. We can do a pinned version and scheduled upgrades.

[15:48] Tom Becker: Back to logs. We also need to know: can you redact PHI from logs? Like, ensure it never logs prompts.

[15:56] Marcus Lin: By default we do not log prompt/response bodies in our application logs. If you enable debug logging, you’d want to keep that off in production. We can also configure log filters in your log collector to be safe.

[16:12] Tom Becker: Okay, and access to logs is controlled by us.

[16:16] Marcus Lin: Correct.

[16:18] Elena Ruiz: For SIEM, we need security events: auth failures, admin role changes, key rotations.

[16:24] Marcus Lin: We can provide events for auth failures, role changes, API key creation/disablement, model deployment actions. Key rotation events are usually from your KMS/Secrets Manager; we don’t manage your keys.

[16:41] Tom Becker: Makes sense.

[16:44] Maya Patel: Let’s talk about request routing/fallback. If a model is overloaded, do you have a fallback model?

[16:50] Colin O'Donnell: In Private, you can define routing policies. Fallback can mean:
- route to a smaller quantized variant
- route to another pool/region
- return a controlled error
But it’s within the deployment boundary you define. If you don’t want any request to leave VPC, then fallback stays inside.

[17:11] Maya Patel: We need that. We can’t fail hard during clinic hours.

[17:15] Colin O'Donnell: Understood.

[17:18] Dr. Priya Nair: If the fallback model is lower quality, do we see that in metrics?

[17:23] Colin O'Donnell: Yes, you’ll see which route/model served the request and you can monitor quality via your eval harness.

[17:31] Elena Ruiz: Do you support A/B tests? We might evaluate two models.

[17:35] Colin O'Donnell: Yes, canary and A/B are part of the console workflows.

[17:41] Tom Becker: What about data residency? We’re US-only.

[17:44] Hannah Schmitt: In Private, it’s in your environment, so residency is your cloud region. No data leaves if you configure it that way.

[17:52] Maya Patel: Great.

[17:54] Elena Ruiz: Okay, sizing question again: We have to plan budget. What’s the minimum viable POC footprint?

[18:01] Colin O'Donnell: For POC, we usually start with one GPU node group sized for the target model, plus CPU nodes for routing and observability. For example, if you test a 13B model, you might do 2–4 A10G/L4. If 70B, you might do 4–8 A100s depending on quantization and context.

[18:21] Elena Ruiz: That’s… a lot.

[18:23] Colin O'Donnell: It is. That’s why collecting the distribution helps: sometimes a tuned 13B is sufficient and drastically cheaper.

[18:31] Dr. Priya Nair: We care about clinical quality though.

[18:34] Colin O'Donnell: Totally. We can help you evaluate quality vs cost, but we’ll be transparent about tradeoffs.

[18:42] Tom Becker: Another security angle: vulnerability scanning and SBOM.

[18:46] Marcus Lin: We can provide SBOM for the Private components under NDA and share our vulnerability management process. Your own container scanning will also apply since it runs in your registry/cluster.

[19:00] Tom Becker: Good.

[19:02] Maya Patel: Okay, let’s shift to network prerequisites checklist. Can you outline exactly what we’d need to provision?

[19:10] Simran Kaur: Sure, at a high level:
- An EKS cluster (or your K8s) with GPU worker nodes
- Internal load balancer for the inference endpoint
- Security groups / NACLs permitting traffic from your app subnets to the service
- Egress allowlist for artifact pulls and optional license/health endpoints
- DNS record(s) and certificates (ACM)
- Log collector/metrics pipeline (Fluent Bit, Prometheus)

[19:41] Elena Ruiz: Any special ports?

[19:43] Simran Kaur: Standard HTTPS 443 to the endpoint. Internally, K8s services; we can provide exact port list. For Splunk HEC it’s whatever your collector uses outbound.

[19:55] Tom Becker: Do you support FIPS mode?

[19:58] Marcus Lin: In AWS, FIPS can apply at OS and library layers. We need to check exact component support. Some customers meet FIPS requirements by using FIPS-enabled AMIs and enforcing TLS policies at the load balancer. Let’s take that as a follow-up because it’s nuanced.

[20:20] Tom Becker: Yeah, okay.

[20:22] Hannah Schmitt: We’ll capture it.

[20:25] Maya Patel: Another question: do you require GPU partitioning or MIG?

[20:30] Colin O'Donnell: We can use MIG in some setups, but it depends on GPU type and performance goals. For long-context, MIG sometimes hurts because memory partitioning becomes the bottleneck. For short QA, MIG can help increase concurrency.

[20:48] Elena Ruiz: So we might do MIG for QA pool, not for summarization.

[20:52] Colin O'Donnell: Exactly.

[20:54] Dr. Priya Nair: How do you prevent one team from consuming all tokens? Like quotas.

[21:00] Colin O'Donnell: Rate limiting and quotas per API key or per project. In Private, you can enforce it at the gateway.

[21:08] Maya Patel: Great.

[21:10] (crosstalk)

[21:11] Tom Becker: Sorry—what about DLP? If a user tries to send PHI to a non-PHI endpoint.

[21:16] Hannah Schmitt: That’s more application layer, but we can help with patterns: separate endpoints, separate credentials, policies.

[21:23] Colin O'Donnell: And you can enforce network segmentation so PHI apps can only reach the Private endpoint.

[21:30] Tom Becker: Perfect.

[21:33] Elena Ruiz: Can you talk about failure modes? If a GPU node dies, what happens?

[21:38] Simran Kaur: K8s reschedules pods, autoscaling can replace nodes. If you have multiple replicas across nodes, traffic shifts. For state like model weights, they’re reloaded; warm-up time can affect latency.

[21:56] Colin O'Donnell: We often recommend N+1 capacity for clinic hours, and a warm pool so TTFT doesn’t spike during re-load.

[22:06] Maya Patel: That’s helpful.

[22:09] Tom Becker: And who has access to the cluster? Do your engineers need it?

[22:13] Simran Kaur: Not by default. Support is usually via your team sharing logs/metrics. If you want, you can provide temporary access via your VPN/bastion, but it’s not required.

[22:27] Tom Becker: We prefer not.

[22:28] Simran Kaur: Totally fine.

[22:31] Maya Patel: Okay, can we cover what you need from us for sizing?

[22:35] Colin O'Donnell: Yes. The best inputs:
- Sample of prompts: not necessarily PHI, but token counts and structure
- Distribution: p50/p95 context length and output length
- Concurrency pattern: steady vs bursts
- Target SLOs: TTFT and total
- Model candidates
If you can’t share prompts, just share token stats.

[23:03] Elena Ruiz: We can share token stats. For prompts, we can generate synthetic.

[23:07] Colin O'Donnell: Perfect.

[23:10] Dr. Priya Nair: Quality evaluation—do you provide an eval harness?

[23:14] Colin O'Donnell: Redwood Optimize has monitoring and regression alerts tied to prompt sets/evals. For Private, we can integrate with your eval framework. We can also provide a basic harness.

[23:28] Maya Patel: Okay.

[23:30] Tom Becker: One more competitor question: We looked at Bedrock. They have “VPC endpoints” but it’s still their managed service. That doesn’t satisfy our PHI requirement.

[23:40] Hannah Schmitt: Yep, that’s the common distinction.

[23:42] Colin O'Donnell: Right. PrivateLink to a managed service is not the same as the service running in your VPC.

[23:49] Tom Becker: Exactly.

[23:52] Maya Patel: So timeline. If we wanted a POC in, say, March, is that realistic?

[23:58] Hannah Schmitt: Potentially yes, depending on whether you need private control plane and the infra readiness. A VPC data plane POC can be stood up in a few weeks with the right prerequisites.

[24:10] Simran Kaur: The gating items are usually networking approvals, egress allowlist, and GPU capacity procurement.

[24:18] Elena Ruiz: GPU capacity is hard.

[24:20] Colin O'Donnell: Understood.

[24:23] (silence)

[24:25] Hannah Schmitt: I’ll pause—what else is top of mind? Tom, anything we didn’t hit?

[24:30] Tom Becker: Two things: evidence for SOC 2 and HIPAA alignment, and what exactly is in audit logs today.

[24:38] Marcus Lin: For SOC 2, we can share the report under NDA and provide a security FAQ addendum. For HIPAA, we generally support customers building HIPAA-compliant systems; we can discuss BAAs depending on commercial terms. For audit logs, I’ll follow up with the current schema and confirm export patterns.

[24:58] Tom Becker: Great.

[25:00] Maya Patel: Elena, anything else?

[25:02] Elena Ruiz: Yeah—API compatibility. We currently use OpenAI-ish schema internally. Do you match that?

[25:08] Colin O'Donnell: We have a straightforward REST/SDK API, and we can support OpenAI-compatible endpoints in some configurations. We should confirm exact features you need: streaming, tool calling, structured output.

[25:22] Elena Ruiz: Streaming yes. Tool calling maybe later.

[25:25] Colin O'Donnell: Okay.

[25:28] Dr. Priya Nair: Also please ensure we can disable any data retention. That’s critical.

[25:33] Hannah Schmitt: Understood.

[25:35] Colin O'Donnell: In Private mode, retention is determined by your environment. We’ll document that clearly.

[25:43] Maya Patel: Okay.

[25:45] Hannah Schmitt: I’m going to do a quick recap and then we’ll end early if we can.

[25:50] Hannah Schmitt: Recap:
1) Private deployment: run inference in Summit VPC, outbound-only by default; no public IPs.
2) Networking: internal LB endpoint; TGW/peering/PrivateLink patterns; you manage DNS + TLS via ACM.
3) Logs: structured JSON; export via Fluent Bit/Otel into Splunk; audit events focus on admin/config, not prompt bodies.
4) KMS: customer-managed keys; volumes encrypted; HSM-backed KMS is acceptable framing.
5) Sizing: need token distributions and concurrency to propose GPU footprint; likely separate pools for summarization vs QA.

[26:33] Hannah Schmitt: Next steps we’ll send: Simran will send the reference architecture and network prereqs checklist. Elena/Maya will send us token stats and workload distributions. Colin will come back with sizing assumptions for a POC. Marcus will confirm audit log schema + Splunk forwarding pattern and capture the FIPS question.

[26:55] Maya Patel: Sounds good.

[26:57] Tom Becker: Yep.

[26:58] Elena Ruiz: Works.

[27:00] Dr. Priya Nair: Thank you.

[27:02] Hannah Schmitt: Great. We’ll follow up over email and schedule the next call.

[27:06] (Call ends)

Note: Transcript truncated by Fireflies export settings after recap; remaining time in calendar block was left unused.
